subtopics.name: Cloud Roles and Agreements
subtopics.definition: Cloud roles name the parties in a cloud service, such as consumer, provider, broker, carrier and auditor; agreements set out what each must do.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Shared duties work only when written down and checked, or the customer cannot know which risks are still its own.
how_it_works: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) names the five actors below; one organization can play several.
Contracts should set service targets and cover data location, breach notification and deleting data at exit.
Independent proof includes a System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 report; here SOC is a report, not Domain 5's security operations center.
Another is certification to the security standard of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), ISO/IEC 27001.

types.meaning: The organization or person that uses the cloud service and owns its data and accounts.
The organization that runs the cloud infrastructure and makes the service available.
A go-between that combines, manages or adds value to services from several providers.
The network or telecom provider that carries traffic between consumers and providers.
An independent party that assesses cloud services and controls and reports on them.

subtopics.example: A small accounting firm is choosing an online document service. Rosa, a junior IT coordinator, requests the provider's latest independent security report and its service level agreement, and notes that the contract says nothing about deleting data at exit. Rosa passes the findings to the managing partner, who decides whether to sign.

review: Read the draft agreement against a checklist of required clauses
Compare the assurance report's scope and date with the services used
evidence: Draft contract with its uptime and support commitments
Exit plan for retrieving and deleting records
audit_focus.recommend: Pass contract gaps and outdated assurance reports to the business owner before signing or renewal.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts contract gaps within tolerance; senior management decides beyond it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Get it in writing and get evidence: the agreement says who does what, and independent reports show the provider does its part.

exam_traps.trap: A provider's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate leaves the customer no security work.
exam_traps.why: It covers only the provider's own controls in its stated scope, not the customer's settings or data.

exam_traps.trap: The service level agreement guarantees no downtime.
exam_traps.why: It sets a target, such as 99.9% availability, and a remedy such as service credits; outages still happen.

key_terms.definition: A contract section setting measurable service targets and the remedies when they are missed.
System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2: an independent auditor's report on a provider's security controls, plus chosen extras such as availability.

subtopics.memory_aid: Write it down, then prove it.

subtopics.name: Protecting Data in the Cloud
subtopics.definition: Protecting cloud data means classifying it, encrypting it in transit and at rest, controlling the keys, and making sure it can be recovered and fully deleted.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The data stays the customer's responsibility in every model, and well-controlled encryption limits the damage if storage is exposed.
how_it_works: Classify data before it moves, so the most sensitive gets the strongest controls or stays out.
Encrypt data in transit with Transport Layer Security (TLS), and at rest with the provider's service or the customer's own tools.
Keys can be provider-managed, customer-managed inside the provider's key service, or held only by the customer.
Keep independent backups, because many services restore deleted or ransomed files only for a short window.
At exit, customers cannot wipe the provider's disks, so they delete data and destroy its keys.

rows.label: Who controls the keys
cells: The customer, inside the provider's key service

rows.label: If the customer loses the keys
cells: Not an issue; the provider holds them

subtopics.example: A marketing agency keeps client files in an online file-sharing service. Ransomware hits through a compromised staff account, and the provider can restore only 30 days of versions. Sofia, a junior IT technician, runs the restore as the incident response lead directs and records, for the lessons-learned review, that there was no separate backup.

review: Identify who controls each encryption key
Confirm restores from independent backups have been tested
evidence: Encryption settings for storage and databases
Backup restore test results for cloud data
audit_focus.recommend: Report unencrypted sensitive data or missing backups to the data owner and the service owner.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides classification and key control

subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify, encrypt, control the keys and back up: the data is the customer's job in every model. Lose keys only you hold, and the data is gone.

exam_traps.trap: Data encrypted by the provider is safe from any provider access.
exam_traps.why: If the provider manages the keys, it can technically decrypt; customer-held keys reduce that exposure.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting a cloud file is enough to sanitize the data.
exam_traps.why: Copies remain in backups and replicas. Destroying the encryption keys makes every copy unreadable.

key_terms.definition: Destroying the keys to encrypted data so only unreadable ciphertext remains; often the only purge option in the cloud.
A cloud service that creates, stores, rotates and controls encryption keys.

subtopics.memory_aid: Own the data, own the keys, own the backup.

subtopics.name: Cloud Misconfiguration, CSPM and CASB
subtopics.definition: A cloud misconfiguration is a setting that leaves resources more exposed than intended, such as public storage, open ports or excessive permissions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Misconfiguration is among the commonest causes of cloud data exposure, because self-service lets anyone create resources quickly.
how_it_works: Common mistakes are public storage, management ports open to the internet and accounts with more rights than they need.
Secure configuration baselines, such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks for cloud platforms, describe good settings.
Cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools scan accounts continuously, compare settings to the baseline and flag drift.
A cloud access security broker (CASB) sits between users and cloud services, showing which are in use and enforcing data rules.

rows.label: Looks at
cells: The organization's own cloud account settings
How users use cloud services, including unapproved ones

rows.label: Finds
cells: Public storage, open ports, weak settings
Shadow IT, risky sharing, data moving to unapproved apps

rows.label: Typical action
cells: Alert, or fix the setting back to the baseline
Block, warn or apply data protection rules

subtopics.example: A research group makes a cloud storage bucket public to share survey files with a partner, and the university's CSPM tool flags it within an hour. Wen, a junior cloud security analyst, confirms it holds student names, notifies the bucket owner and security manager under the incident procedure, and records when exposure began.

review: Check whether your procedure assigns you a finding before acting on it
Identify unapproved cloud apps from broker reports
evidence: CSPM findings with dates found and fixed
Cloud activity logs showing who changed a setting
audit_focus.recommend: Fix baseline failures your procedure assigns you, recording the change; send others to the resource owner, and escalate exposed sensitive data as an incident.
audit_focus.decides: The resource owner assigns the fix; the risk owner accepts within tolerance, senior management beyond

subtopics.isaca_rule: In the cloud, the likeliest breach is the customer's own setting. Use baselines and continuous checks, fix the drift your procedure assigns you, and report exposed sensitive data fast, because exposure time matters.

exam_traps.trap: If a storage bucket was public, the provider caused the breach.
exam_traps.why: Storage permissions are a customer setting in every service model.

exam_traps.trap: A CASB does the same job as a network firewall.
exam_traps.why: A firewall filters by network rules; a CASB understands cloud apps, users and data, so it can spot shadow IT.

key_terms.definition: Technology, such as cloud apps, that staff use for work without IT or security approval.
Gradual, often unapproved changes that move a system's settings away from its approved baseline.
Defining infrastructure in reviewed files deployed like software, so mistakes are caught before go-live.

subtopics.memory_aid: Check settings before attackers do: baseline, scan, fix, report.

subtopics.name: Shared Responsibility for AI Workloads
subtopics.definition: Shared responsibility for cloud-hosted artificial intelligence (AI) workloads splits duties: the provider secures the AI platform; the customer secures data, models, access and use.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Teams that assume the provider secures everything leave training data, tuned models and access settings exposed.
how_it_works: The split follows the service model, as the table shows; data and access always stay with the customer.
Training data and tuned models are customer assets needing access control, encryption and logging.
Apps built on a hosted model need the customer's own input and output filtering.
Check the terms first: are prompts (what users send) stored, and do they train the provider's models?
Never paste sensitive data into public AI tools; 5.1.8 covers that lesson.

rows.label: Customer secures
cells: Users, settings, prompts and data entered
Training data, tuned models, app code and settings
Operating system, AI frameworks, models, data and access

rows.label: Example
cells: A chat assistant used by staff
A hosted model the company builds an app on
Graphics processing unit (GPU) servers for training a model

subtopics.example: A retailer fine-tunes a model on a cloud AI platform using customers' purchase histories. Marco, a junior cloud analyst, finds the storage holding the training data and the tuned model open to every developer account. A colleague says the provider secures the platform, so it is fine. Marco checks the provider's responsibility guide, confirms access to that data is the customer's duty, and reports it to the platform owner.

review: Check AI storage for access wider than the team that needs it
Use only AI services on the approved list
evidence: Role assignments on AI buckets, exported from the console
Contract clauses on prompt retention for each AI vendor
audit_focus.recommend: Report open access to training data or models to the platform owner, and unapproved AI services to the security manager.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves the AI policy and tools; data owners decide what data may be used

subtopics.isaca_rule: An AI service is still a cloud service: the provider secures the platform, and the customer owns its data, models, access and settings.

exam_traps.trap: The AI provider secures the training data because it sits on its platform.
exam_traps.why: The provider secures the platform underneath; who can reach data and models on it is a customer setting.

exam_traps.trap: A model the company tuned itself is just a file.
exam_traps.why: A tuned model carries patterns from its training data and can leak them.

key_terms.definition: Further training a ready-made model on an organization's own data, making the tuned model a sensitive asset.
Contract terms saying whether a provider stores inputs, for how long, and whether they train its models.

key_terminologies.Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model: A seven-layer reference model that splits network communication into separate jobs, from physical signals to applications.
key_terminologies.TCP/IP model: The Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol model the internet runs on, in four layers: Link, Internet, Transport and Application.
key_terminologies.Media access control (MAC) address: A hardware ID used to deliver frames within one local network; not the same as mandatory access control (MAC) in Domain 3.
key_terminologies.Internet Protocol (IP) address: A logical address that routers use to move packets between networks; IPv4 is 32-bit and IPv6 is 128-bit.
key_terminologies.Port: A number from 0 to 65535 that tells a host which service should receive traffic.
key_terminologies.Transmission Control Protocol (TCP): A connection-based transport protocol that delivers data reliably and in order.
key_terminologies.User Datagram Protocol (UDP): A connectionless transport protocol that is fast but does not guarantee delivery.
key_terminologies.Transport Layer Security (TLS): Encrypts and authenticates connections, such as HTTPS (secure web browsing); use version 1.2 or 1.3, never the retired Secure Sockets Layer (SSL).
key_terminologies.Secure Shell (SSH): An encrypted protocol for remote command-line access and file transfer, replacing Telnet.
key_terminologies.Virtual private network (VPN): An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network.
key_terminologies.Firewall: A device or software that allows or blocks traffic between networks or hosts by rules.
key_terminologies.Intrusion detection system (IDS): A tool that watches network traffic or hosts and alerts on signs of attack, without blocking it.
key_terminologies.Intrusion prevention system (IPS): Sits in the traffic path and can block suspicious activity.
key_terminologies.Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3): The current Wi-Fi security standard; its Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) sign-in resists offline password guessing.
key_terminologies.Industrial control system (ICS): Embedded and networked computers that run physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.
key_terminologies.Internet of Things (IoT): Everyday network-connected devices, such as cameras and sensors, that collect data or act with little human input.
key_terminologies.Network segmentation: Dividing a network into parts with controlled traffic between them.
key_terminologies.Screened subnet (DMZ): A zone for public-facing servers between the internet and internal networks; also called a demilitarized zone (DMZ).
key_terminologies.Virtual local area network (VLAN): A logical network carved out of a shared physical switch network.
key_terminologies.Micro-segmentation: Security policy applied to individual workloads, limiting each to the connections it needs.
key_terminologies.Defense in depth: Layering independent physical, technical and administrative controls so one failure does not expose the asset.
key_terminologies.Zero Trust: An approach that grants no trust based on network location and checks every request to every resource.
key_terminologies.Network access control (NAC): Checking a connecting user and device, and the device's health, before granting network access.
key_terminologies.Cloud computing: Using computing resources from a shared pool over a network, taking more or less as needed.
key_terminologies.Cloud characteristics: The five essential traits of cloud computing: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.
key_terminologies.IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: Cloud service models: infrastructure as a service (rented servers), platform as a service (a managed platform for code) and software as a service (a ready app).
key_terminologies.Public, private, community, hybrid cloud: Cloud deployment models, defined by who the infrastructure is built for and shared with.
key_terminologies.Shared responsibility model: Provider secures the cloud itself, the customer what it puts there; the split shifts by service model, but data, identities and access stay the customer's.
key_terminologies.Cloud access security broker (CASB): Sits between users and cloud services to show use and enforce policy.
key_terminologies.Cloud security posture management (CSPM): Continuously checks cloud settings against a secure baseline.
